meta.description: Clayton Christensen said it — but the usual citation is to the wrong book. What the sources actually show, and what they don't.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It's easier to hold to your principles 100% of the time than it is to hold to them 98% of the time'?
meta.ogDescription: Clayton Christensen, certainly. From The Innovator's Dilemma or How Will You Measure Your Life? — that is genuinely unsettled.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1952–2020 · Harvard Business School professor & author of The Innovator’s Dilemma
answer.sourceLine: The line is Christensen’s — that much is not in question, and no competing claimant exists. The source is another matter. Wikiquote files it under The Innovator’s Dilemma ↗ while noting it comes from the introduction to the 2012 edition — so not from the 1997 book the heading names. Elsewhere it is routinely credited to How Will You Measure Your Life? instead. We could not open either text to settle it.

source.heading: Right author, unsettled book

source.excerpt: It’s easier to hold to your principles 100% of the time than it is to hold to them 98% of the time.
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced Christensen page ↗ carries the sentence in this wording, under a section headed The Innovator’s Dilemma (1997), with the single-line citation ‘Intro (2012 edition)’.

Those two labels contradict each other, and that is our own observation rather than anything the page says: a book first published in 1997 cannot contain the introduction written for its 2012 edition, so the heading and the sub-note cannot both be describing the source.

The competing citation — to How Will You Measure Your Life? — appears widely in quote collections, but we were unable to fetch any of those pages from this run, so none of them is linked here and none is being relied on.

Neither primary text could be read: hbr.org refused the connection outright, and the Internet Archive’s scan of How Will You Measure Your Life? ↗ is access-restricted, with search-inside unavailable. The citation stays open rather than being guessed.
source.excerptNote: No fuller passage is printed here on purpose. Reproducing the surrounding paragraph would mean copying it from a text we could not open, and a plausible-looking context is exactly the kind of filler this site exists to avoid. The sentence above is the whole of what the sources we could read actually carry.

author.name: Clayton Christensen
author.heading: About Clayton Christensen
author.metaLine: 1952–2020 · Harvard Business School professor & theorist of disruptive innovation
author.bio: Clayton Magleby Christensen (born Salt Lake City, 6 April 1952; died Boston, 23 January 2020) was the Kim B. Clark Professor of Business Administration at Harvard Business School. He coined disruptive innovation in a 1995 article and developed it in The Innovator’s Dilemma (1997), which The Economist cited in calling him the most influential management thinker of his time. He wrote as readily about how to live as about how firms fail, and the two quotations here come from that second strand.

misattribution.heading: Which book is it from?
misattribution.intro: Nobody is falsely credited here. The error in circulation is about the source, not the speaker.

items.why: This is how Wikiquote files it ↗, and the citation travels in that form. But the entry’s own sub-note says ‘Intro (2012 edition)’, which rules out the 1997 first edition that the date in the heading points to.

Widely repeated, and entirely plausible — the 2010 essay of that title argues at length for exactly this position. We could not open the essay or the book to confirm the sentence appears in either, so we are not asserting it.

misattribution.truthLine: What can be said without guessing: the words are Christensen’s, and the book they came from has not been established here.

context.heading: Why 100 beats 98
lead: The argument is in the arithmetic, and it is not the arithmetic you expect. A rule you keep 98% of the time sounds like a rule with a sensible allowance in it. What it actually is, on Christensen’s reading, is a rule you have to re-decide every single time it is tested — because once an exception exists, every new case is a candidate for it.

A rule kept 100% of the time is decided once, in the calm, and never argued again. That is the whole claim: the stricter line is the cheaper one to hold, because it removes the negotiation rather than the behaviour.
context.detailsSummary: A note on what this page does not claim
context.pull: An exception is not an allowance. It is a standing invitation to re-open the question.

Clayton Christensen was born 6 April 1952 and died 23 January 2020; he was the Kim B. Clark Professor of Business Administration at Harvard Business School and coined 'disruptive innovation'.
